question: What does the Single Responsibility Principle (SRP) mean in the context of React components?

options.text: A component should accept only one prop
options.explanation: The number of props is not related to SRP. A component can accept many props and still have a single responsibility.

options.text: A component should contain no more than 100 lines of code
options.explanation: Line count is a heuristic, not the principle itself. SRP is about responsibility, not size.

options.text: A component must not use useState
options.explanation: useState is a normal part of a component. SRP does not prohibit using hooks.

options.text: A component should have only one reason to change
options.explanation: This is the SRP formulation: if a component needs to change due to UI changes, loading logic, and business rules — it has three reasons to change, which violates SRP.

question: Which of the following statements are true for Presentational (Dumb) components?

options.text: They do not make API requests
options.explanation: API requests are the responsibility of Container (Smart) components.

options.text: They cannot have any state
options.explanation: Presentational components can have UI state: dropdown open/closed, active tab. The restriction applies to data state, not UI state.

options.text: They are easier to test than Smart components
options.explanation: To test a Dumb component, you just pass the required props — no need to mock APIs or context.

options.text: All of the above options are incorrect
options.explanation: Some of the listed options are indeed correct.

options.text: They receive data via props
options.explanation: Presentational components do not know about data sources — they receive everything via props.

question: You have an OrderPage component of 400 lines: it loads an order, shows details, allows canceling the order, and shows change history. What is the best way to decompose it?

options.text: Split into OrderContainer (loading/logic) and OrderView (display)
options.explanation: This is better, but not enough. OrderView will still be large and have multiple responsibilities.

options.text: Leave as is — decomposition will complicate the code
options.explanation: 400 lines with four areas of responsibility is a clear candidate for decomposition. Complexity will only grow.

options.text: Create a separate file for each function inside the component
options.explanation: Moving functions to separate files does not solve the problem of a single component managing everything.

options.text: Split into OrderContainer + OrderDetails + CancelOrderForm + OrderHistory
options.explanation: Each component has one responsibility: data loading, showing details, cancel form, history. This is correct decomposition by responsibilities.

question: What is 'prop drilling' and why is it a problem?

options.text: Passing handler functions as props
options.explanation: Passing callbacks is normal React practice, not prop drilling.

options.text: Passing too many props to a single component
options.explanation: This is a different problem — a wide component interface. Prop drilling is about passing through intermediate components.

options.text: Passing props through many levels of components that don't use them themselves
options.explanation: When userId passes through Page → Layout → Sidebar → Menu → Avatar, and Page, Layout, Sidebar, and Menu don't use it — that's prop drilling. Intermediate components know about foreign data.

options.text: Using the spread operator when passing props
options.explanation: Spread when passing props is a separate practice, not related to prop drilling.

question: In which cases should you decompose a component?

options.text: The component is hard to describe in one sentence without using 'and'
options.explanation: If you have to say 'loads data AND shows a form AND validates' — that's multiple responsibilities.

options.text: The component contains a single useState hook
options.explanation: One useState is not a reason for decomposition. This is normal for a small component.

options.text: All of the above options are incorrect
options.explanation: Some of the listed options are indeed correct.

options.text: A new developer cannot understand the component in 30 seconds
options.explanation: Readability is an important criterion. If it takes a long time to figure out what a component does — it's time to decompose.

options.text: The component is used in two different places in the application
options.explanation: Reusability is one of the key signals for decomposition. Better to extract a component before duplication appears.

question: A ProductCard component receives a product object as a whole. Inside, it only uses product.name and product.price. What is better?

options.text: Pass only name and price as separate props
options.explanation: Minimal interface is better. The component depends only on what it uses. Easier to test, easier to refactor.

options.text: Use React.memo for optimization
options.explanation: memo solves performance issues, not the problem of excessive dependencies in props.

options.text: Leave as is — passing the whole object is more convenient
options.explanation: Passing extra data complicates testing and makes dependencies implicit. The component knows about fields it doesn't use.

options.text: Destructure the object inside the component
options.explanation: Destructuring inside the component doesn't change the signature — it still depends on the whole product object.

question: Which of the following violates the Single Responsibility Principle?

options.text: A Button component changes style on hover via useState
options.explanation: Managing hover state via state is normal button UI-state, not an SRP violation.

options.text: A Modal component manages its open/closed state
options.explanation: Modal UI state (open/closed) is a normal responsibility of the Modal component itself.

options.text: A Form component simultaneously validates data, sends it to the server, and shows the result
options.explanation: Three different responsibilities: validation, sending, displaying results. Better to separate or extract logic into hooks.

options.text: A UserList component simultaneously loads users via fetch and renders their list
options.explanation: Data loading and display are different responsibilities. Should be split into UserListContainer and UserListView.

question: What is the main practical benefit of separating into Container and Presentational components?

options.text: Automatic performance optimization
options.explanation: The pattern doesn't add automatic optimization — it's an architectural decision for readability and testability.

options.text: Reduced number of re-renders
options.explanation: This is not the main goal of the pattern. For render optimization, memo, useMemo, and useCallback are used.

options.text: Presentational components can be tested without API mocks
options.explanation: This is the main practical benefit. A Dumb component is tested simply: pass props — check output. No mocks, providers, or fetch needed.

options.text: Reduced bundle size
options.explanation: Splitting into Container/Presentational does not affect bundle size — the amount of code is roughly the same.

question: When should you NOT decompose a component?

options.text: When the component is hard to cover with a test
options.explanation: Testing difficulty is a signal for decomposition, not a reason to avoid it.

options.text: When the component is used in three places
options.explanation: Reusability is a good reason to decompose. This is exactly when decomposition is justified.

options.text: When multiple developers are working on the component simultaneously
options.explanation: Team work on one large file is an additional argument FOR decomposition, not against.

options.text: When the component contains 80 lines of JSX with a single logical area
options.explanation: 80 lines with a single clear area of responsibility is fine. Decomposition for the sake of decomposition complicates code without benefit.

question: You are refactoring a Dashboard component. The DataTable component has local state for sorting (sortField, sortDir). Is this a violation of the Presentational component pattern?

options.text: You need to lift the state up and pass it via props
options.explanation: Lifting sorting state to the Dashboard level is unnecessary — the parent shouldn't know about table display details.

options.text: No, UI state (sorting, active tab) is acceptable in a Presentational component
options.explanation: Sorting is UI behavior of the table, not business data. Storing sortField/sortDir in DataTable is correct: the component manages its own display.

options.text: Yes, any state violates the Presentational component pattern
options.explanation: This is a common misconception. Presentational components can have UI state — state that relates to display, not to data.

options.text: It depends on the number of fields in state
options.explanation: The number of fields doesn't define pattern violation. What matters is the nature of the state: UI or data.
